elements.text: This is the nature of c++ templates. The array_slice (generalization of data_slice) is a template. The compiler only requires that the template parameter satisfy all of its compiled uses.

elements.text:
Hmm. So lets say I declare "data_chunk myChunk", fill it  with several bytes of entropy and use it as argument in "bitcoin_short_hash(data_slice data);" 

When that hash function is called, and the input is a data_chunk instead of data_slice, the implicit conversion happens, using the single argument constructor with template <typename Container>

The template for array_slice will take "data_chunk" as "Container type".
 
And so the array_slice constructor will be: array_slice(const data_chunk& container) for this implicit conversion.

text:
Hmm. So lets say I declare "data_chunk myChunk", fill it  with several bytes of entropy and use it as argument in "bitcoin_short_hash(data_slice data);" 

When that hash function is called, and the input is a data_chunk instead of data_slice, the implicit conversion happens, using the single argument constructor with template <typename Container>

The template for array_slice will take "data_chunk" as "Container type".
 
And so the array_slice constructor will be: array_slice(const data_chunk& container) for this implicit conversion.

elements.text: And as you have surmised, all of the requirements of the Container type are here:
begin_(container.data()), end_(container.data() + container.size())

text: And as you have surmised, all of the requirements of the Container type are here:   `begin_(container.data()), end_(container.data() + container.size())`
